docs.title: Home
docs.text:
What is Guic

Guic (Graphical User Interface Creator) is a library for building graphical user interfaces. Its purpose is to make interface creation easier for software: no need to deploy heavy frameworks, memorize graphics libraries, or study the one right architectural approach.

Guic runs on the SDL engine, which makes it suitable for production: the interface won't lag from a couple of images. The library is distributed under the LGPL-3.0 license with an exception (see the distribution for details), so you can develop commercial software with a clear conscience.

Guic stands out with an intuitive base of primitive elements. The interface is assembled like a constructor: simple elements form full-fledged components with their own logic, and those components form an interface of any complexity. It grows step by step, from a simple application background and a selection menu to complex composite structures. Built-in tools help development by applying common interface patterns.

An interface needs a loop to be displayed, but Guic won't make you spend long thinking about how to fill it. User-interaction elements can take passed lambda functions, which makes it possible to attach functionality outside the main loop.

Want your own Resource, Event or Element? You can extend the library. The engine handles everything you expose in the public and protected interface of your derived class.

Let's get started

docs.title: The data union
docs.text:
A union with the event data. Which field is relevant depends on type:

  • key - the key and the repeat flag. Guic does not currently fill the pressed and released flags
  • mouse - the coordinates x, y, the offset dx, dy, the key and the wheel scroll wheel
  • click - the press positions pressedX, pressedY, the release positions releasedX, releasedY and the key. Filled for MouseButtonClicked
  • window - the position x, y and the size w, h of the window. Guic does not currently fill the close flag
  • text - the entered text as a char[32] array
  • file - the number of files count. Guic does not currently fill this field: the file paths are in filePaths

docs.title: guic::Font
docs.text: A font resource class – loads a font from a file at the given size, builds a glyph atlas and stores kerning. Inherits engine::Resource

docs.title: Constructors
docs.text: • Font(const std::string& path, Uint32 font_size) - Constructor for creating a font from the file at path with size font_size

docs.title: Pack structure
docs.text:
A set of character codepoints to be loaded into the atlas. Stores the list codepoints. Methods: contains(Uint32 codepoint) - checks whether a codepoint is present, size() - the number of codepoints, make(const std::string& characters) - creates a set from a string of characters.

The service constant MissingGlyphCodepoint (0xFFFFFFFF) is private and not exposed. It is used for the placeholder glyph that replaces a character missing from the loaded sets.

docs.title: Functions in namespace guic
docs.text:
• void guic_delay(Uint32 mls) - Suspends execution for mls milliseconds
  • Position guic_get_mouse_pos() - Returns the current position of the mouse cursor
  • void guic_send_event(Event*& event) - Puts an event into the Guic queue. If event is nullptr, nothing happens. Otherwise Guic takes ownership of the event and sets the pointer event to nullptr. The event becomes available through config::guic_poll_event() after the next config::guic_update_events() stable

docs.title: Functions in namespace guic::config
docs.text:
• bool guic_init() - Initializes Guic. Returns true on successful initialization. A repeated call while Guic is already initialized does nothing and also returns true. Returns false if SDL or TTF could not be initialized
  • bool guic_quit() - Shuts down Guic. Returns true on successful shutdown, false if Guic was not initialized
  • void guic_update_events() - Removes the events of the previous batch and fetches a new batch: events from the system and events passed through guic_send_event. Pointers obtained from guic_poll_event() before this call become invalid stable
  • const Event* guic_poll_event() - Returns the next event of the current batch, or nullptr if the events have run out. The event belongs to Guic and is valid until the next guic_update_events() stable

Usually events are handled by Window in the tune() method, and the application does not need these functions directly.

docs.title: guic::Image
docs.text: A picture resource class – loads an image from a file and passes it to the renderer. Inherits engine::Resource

docs.title: Supported formats
docs.text:
Images are loaded with stb_image. The format is detected from the file content, not from the extension.

  • PNG
  • JPEG
  • BMP
  • GIF - only the first frame; animation is not supported
  • TGA
  • PSD - the flattened image; layers are not read
  • HDR - converted to 8-bit
  • PIC
  • PNM - binary PPM and PGM only

Not supported: SVG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF and other formats. For them the image is not loaded.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Type Method Purpose Label void load Queues a resource (Resource) for loading. The loading actually happens in flush(), which is called by present() stable void unload Queues a resource for unloading. Performed in flush() before the loads stable bool isLoaded Checks whether the resource is loaded into the renderer in its current version stable void flush Applies the deferred unloads, then the loads. For loading, the pixels are taken through resource->load(), copied into an atlas page, after which resource->unload() is called, so no copy remains in CPU memory stable void draw Draws geometry (std::vector<Vertex>) without a texture beta void draw Queues drawing of geometry with the texture of the given resource. If the resource is not loaded, it is queued for loading beta void clear Clears the whole renderer buffer with the given Color. The clipping area is not taken into account stable void clearClip Fills the current clipping area with black. The clipping area itself does not change stable void present Applies the queued loads and unloads (flush) and shows the drawn frame. Drawing commands are grouped by atlases stable void setClipRect Sets the clipping area beta Rect getClippedRect Returns the current clipping area beta Size getMaxTextureSize Returns the maximum texture size supported by the renderer stable

docs.title: guic::engine::Resource
docs.text: The base class of resources (images, fonts) that Renderer loads. Descendants, such as Image and Font, implement createBitmap(), which builds the pixels of the resource. The pixel cache is managed by Resource itself.

docs.title: Constructors and destructor
docs.text:
• Resource() - Default constructor stable
  • Resource(const Resource&), operator=(const Resource&) - Deleted: a resource cannot be copied. The cache is moved between resources by pull() stable
  • ~Resource() - Virtual destructor stable

docs.title: Public methods
docs.text: Type Method Purpose Label const Bitmap* load Returns the resource's pixels from the cache. If there is no cache, or the version has changed and there are no active references, builds it through createBitmap(). Each call increments the cache reference count; a paired call is unload() stable void unload Decrements the cache reference count. When the count reaches zero, the pixels are freed stable bool isMetadataLoaded Checks whether the resource's metadata is loaded stable Uint32 getRevision Returns the version of the resource's content. The version increases when the content changes; Renderer reloads the resource when the versions diverge stable Uint32 getCacheRevision Returns the version for which the current pixel cache was built stable bool pull(Resource*& src) Takes the cache and metadata from the resource src, if it has exactly one cache reference and the current resource has no references. Afterwards src is deleted and the pointer is set to null. Needed to replace a resource without reloading its pixels stable

docs.title: Protected methods
docs.text: Type Method Purpose Label Bitmap* createBitmap() = 0 Pure virtual. Builds the pixels of the resource. Implemented in descendants; the result is cached by Resource stable void nextRevision Increments the resource's version, signalling the renderer that a reload is needed stable bool copyMetadataFrom(Resource& src) Copies the metadata from src during pull. The base class copies nothing and returns true. Descendants override the method stable

docs.title: Event routing in tune()
docs.text:
• Events from the Guic queue are passed to the window with a matching winId. An event with winId 0 is passed to all windows.
  • The WindowResized event changes the size of the window's root container.
  • MouseMoved is passed to the element under the cursor. The window remembers this element as the last one the cursor worked with.
  • Other mouse events (presses, releases, wheel) are passed to the element under the cursor.
  • MouseButtonClicked is passed to an element only if the press and the release happened over the same element.
  • Other events are passed to the window's root container through control.
  • WindowClosed closes the window, unless closeEventSkip() was called.

The free functions for the event queue (guic_send_event, config::guic_update_events, config::guic_poll_event) are described on the Functions page.

docs.title: Creating a window
docs.text:
To use Guic, include the Guic.hpp header – it contains all the main definitions for working with the library.

#include <Guic/Guic.hpp>

All elements live in the guic namespace, so for convenience we'll use using.

using namespace guic;

Add the main function, and in it create a new window with the Window class, specifying its title and size. For the size we use the Guic class Size.

int main() {
    Window window("What's your mood?", Size(640, 480));

    return 0;
}

A window is created closed at first, so we open it (it will be shown automatically when opened).

window.open();

Guic does not manage the program loop, so we create the loop ourselves. The loop condition can check whether the window is open.

while (window.isOpen()) {

}

The window has two functions for control – tune and display. Tune processes incoming events and runs element logic, while display collects all changes and sends them for drawing. Add them to the loop in a logical order – first the logic processing, then the drawing:

window.tune();
window.display();

The loop eats as much CPU as it can get. To save resources, add a delay at the end of the loop:

guic_delay(10);

docs.title: Final result
docs.text:
#include <Guic/Guic.hpp>

using namespace guic;

int main() {
    Window window("What's your mood?", Size(640, 480));
    window.open();

    while (window.isOpen()) {
        window.tune();
        window.display();

        guic_delay(10);
    }

    return 0;
}
Next step – Drawing an image

docs.title: Custom element
docs.text:
Containers are great! But if this goes on, our main will be as tall as the Eiffel Tower. Guic has a tool that suits us - the Composite. In essence, a Composite is a bundle of several elements into one more complex element. It can have its own logic and drawing, but the idea is always the same - tie elements together into one node.

The "Reset" button practically begs to become a new composite, so we start with it. Create a class "ResetButton" and inherit from the Composite element. The constructor takes a Rect and a font.

  • Note - we pass the font by reference. Font is a descendant of Resource, and copying a Resource is forbidden. So passing the font by value (Font font) will cause a compilation error.
class ResetButton : public Composite {
public:
    ResetButton(Rect rect, Font& font) : Composite(rect) {

    }
private:

};

The "Reset" button consists of a background, a text and a trigger. Move all these elements from main into private:

Sprite resetShape;
Text resetCaption;
Trigger reset;

Now they need to be initialized in the constructor. Again we change the positions of the elements, neatly adjusting their appearance.

resetShape.setRect(Rect(0, 0, 140, 50));
resetShape.setColor(Color("#f4e1c1"));
resetShape.setRadius(25);

resetCaption.setRect(Rect(35, 16, 100, 30));
resetCaption.setString("Reset");
resetCaption.setFont(font);
resetCaption.setColor(Color("#1b4242"));

reset.setRect(Rect(0, 0, 140, 50));
reset.setRadius(25);
reset.onLMB([](){ likes = 0; });

Now we need to give Guic the ability to manage these elements. We will use add - the element is added to the composite's own container and is managed automatically. Add them at the end of the constructor, and do not forget the order: Background -> Caption -> Trigger

add(resetShape);
add(resetCaption);
add(reset);

Everything is ready. Now we have a fully working "Reset button" element. Let's create it in main, before the likes counter text, and add it to our window

ResetButton resetButton(Rect(460, 400, 140, 50), font);
window.add(resetButton);

Now let's remove the old code from the previous step from main: the container together with its elements (resetShape, resetCaption, reset, total) and the call container.show() in the loop. Otherwise the reset button will appear twice.

The counter now lies directly in the window again, in the top-left corner:

Text total(Rect(25, 40, 280, 40), "Likes today: 0", font);
total.setColor(Color::White);
window.add(total);

In the loop we remove container.show() - only the update of the counter text remains.

We remove the picture of the cat, the trigger and the "Need coffee" text from main - they will be replaced by a mood card. This looks like a foretaste of the mood card! We create a class MoodCard. It will take a picture, a font and the mood description. Do not forget to pass resources by reference. The mood description will be const, so that we can pass "text as strings"

class MoodCard : public Composite {
public:
    MoodCard(Rect rect, Image& picture, Font& font, const std::string& mood) : Composite(rect) {

    }

private:

};

We pull our elements out of main and add them to private. We will also add a "Background" sprite here, so the card looks nicer

Sprite background;
Sprite photo;
Text caption;
Trigger heart;

We initialize our elements, except, for now, the trigger:

background.setRect(Rect(0, 0, rect.width, rect.height));
background.setColor(Color("#f4e1c1"));
background.setRadius(36);

photo.setRect(Rect(20, 20, 140, 140));
photo.setImage(picture);
photo.setRadius(70);

caption.setRect(Rect(20, 170, 140, 50));
caption.setString(mood);
caption.setFont(font);
caption.setColor(Color("#1b4242"));

The trigger must add the number of presses to the likes counter. Besides, the code above shifted the cards so that they overlap each other. This can get in the way of seeing the text, so when the cat is clicked, we will bring the element to the top.

In Guic, the elements above are determined either by the drawing order or by layers. Elements in a container are drawn in the order they were added, so we can simply re-add the element. Let's create a pointer to it in private and a function to fill it.

void setContainer(Container &container) {
    this->container = &container;
}

private:
    Container* container = nullptr;
  • P.S. Giving elements access to their parents is not recommended - starting with the fact that an element can end up in an infinite loop, and ending with undefined behavior of Guic. So far nothing like this has been noticed (except for the UNSTABLE members of the classes), but in serious projects it is better to avoid such a design.

Now we can initialize the trigger itself

heart.setRect(Rect(20, 20, 140, 140));
heart.setRadius(70);
heart.onLMB([this] {
    likes++;
    if(container == nullptr) return; // Just in case
    container->remove(*this);
    container->add(*this);
});

Hand control over to the composite

add(background);
add(photo);
add(caption);
add(heart);

The element is ready! Now we can use them in main. Before the reset button, we create our card elements, create a container for them, add the cards to it, and put the container into the window. Do not forget to call our function that sets the card's container.

MoodCard happy(Rect(0, 0, 180, 230), picture, font, "Feeling bright,\nlike morning tea");
MoodCard tired(Rect(150, 0, 180, 230), picture, font, "A bit tired,\nbut holding on");
MoodCard coffee(Rect(300, 0, 180, 230), picture, font, "Need coffee\nand some quiet");

Container cards(Rect(30, 110, 580, 230));

cards.add(happy);
happy.setContainer(cards);

cards.add(tired);
tired.setContainer(cards);

cards.add(coffee);
coffee.setContainer(cards);

window.add(cards);

  • P.S. You can override some functions of a composite to hook into their logic. You can see the list of virtual functions on the Composite page.

  • P.S.S. So far we have covered only the method of creating an element through add() - adding an element to the container inside it. The composite, in turn, proxies virtual functions to it. But there is a second way - by adding elements through the adopt and release methods, you bind them to the composite bypassing the container. In that case, you must check ALL virtual methods of the composite and add logic to them if needed.

In the end, main puts everything together: three cards in the cards container, the ResetButton reset button and the likes counter in the top-left corner.

#include <Guic/Guic.hpp>

using namespace guic;

int likes = 0;

class ResetButton : public Composite {
public:
    ResetButton(Rect rect, Font& font) : Composite(rect) {
        resetShape.setRect(Rect(0, 0, 140, 50));
        resetShape.setColor(Color("#f4e1c1"));
        resetShape.setRadius(25);

        resetCaption.setRect(Rect(35, 16, 100, 30));
        resetCaption.setString("Reset");
        resetCaption.setFont(font);
        resetCaption.setColor(Color("#1b4242"));

        reset.setRect(Rect(0, 0, 140, 50));
        reset.setRadius(25);
        reset.onLMB([](){ likes = 0; });

        add(resetShape);
        add(resetCaption);
        add(reset);
    }
private:
    Sprite resetShape;
    Text resetCaption;
    Trigger reset;
};

class MoodCard : public Composite {
public:
    MoodCard(Rect rect, Image& picture, Font& font, const std::string& mood) : Composite(rect) {
        background.setRect(Rect(0, 0, rect.width, rect.height));
        background.setColor(Color("#f4e1c1"));
        background.setRadius(36);

        photo.setRect(Rect(20, 20, 140, 140));
        photo.setImage(picture);
        photo.setRadius(70);

        caption.setRect(Rect(20, 170, 140, 50));
        caption.setString(mood);
        caption.setFont(font);
        caption.setColor(Color("#1b4242"));

        heart.setRect(Rect(20, 20, 140, 140));
        heart.setRadius(70);
        heart.onLMB([this] {
            likes++;
            if(container == nullptr) return;
            container->remove(*this);
            container->add(*this);
        });

        add(background);
        add(photo);
        add(caption);
        add(heart);
    }

    void setContainer(Container &container) {
        this->container = &container;
    }

    Container* container = nullptr;

private:
    Sprite background;
    Sprite photo;
    Text caption;
    Trigger heart;
};

int main() {
    Window window("What's your mood?", Size(640, 480));
    window.open();

    Sprite background(Rect(0, 0, 640, 480), Color("#1b4242"));
    window.add(background);

    Font font("UbuntuMono-Bold.ttf", 16);
    font.addPack(Font::Pack::RU);
    font.addPack(Font::Pack::Sign);

    Text title(Rect(25, 25, 580, 40), "What kind of cat are you today?", font);
    title.setColor(Color::White);
    window.add(title);

    Image picture("kit.png");

    MoodCard happy(Rect(0, 0, 180, 230), picture, font, "Feeling bright,\nlike morning tea");
    MoodCard tired(Rect(150, 0, 180, 230), picture, font, "A bit tired,\nbut holding on");
    MoodCard coffee(Rect(300, 0, 180, 230), picture, font, "Need coffee\nand some quiet");

    Container cards(Rect(30, 110, 580, 230));

    cards.add(happy);
    happy.setContainer(cards);

    cards.add(tired);
    tired.setContainer(cards);

    cards.add(coffee);
    coffee.setContainer(cards);

    window.add(cards);

    ResetButton resetButton(Rect(460, 400, 140, 50), font);
    window.add(resetButton);

    Text total(Rect(25, 40, 280, 40), "Likes today: 0", font);
    total.setColor(Color::White);
    window.add(total);

    int shown = 0;
    while (window.isOpen()) {
        window.tune();

        if (likes != shown) {
            shown = likes;
            total.setString("Likes today: " + std::to_string(likes));
        }

        window.display();

        guic_delay(10);
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Drawing an image
docs.text:
To draw an image, we can take the code from the previous step.

A picture is created with the Sprite class. When creating it, we specify its Rect - the rectangle of the area, where x and y are the coordinates of the sprite, and width and height are its size. The second parameter is the sea-wave color, set through the Guic class Color

Sprite background(Rect(0, 0, 640, 480), Color("#1b4242"));

To display the sprite, we need to add it to the Window (The same element cannot be added to different windows - it will be moved instead)

window.add(background);

Now we can compile the code and see that the sea-wave background is set. If we try to stretch the window, the areas on the right and at the bottom will stay empty, because our background is designed for a 640x480 window, and it is not drawn beyond that

But a colored rectangle is not enough - we can display an image. The Image class does not store the image itself, so it will be loaded into the program automatically when needed. This behavior is typical of any resource class.

Create an Image

Image picture("kit.png");

Now create a Sprite, move it a little, but instead of the sea-wave color, specify our image

Sprite photo(Rect(100, 100, 140, 140), picture);

And for good measure, turn it into a circle. Our sprite is 140 wide. So the circle's diameter will also be 140. Therefore we divide the diameter by 2 and get the needed radius of 70

photo.setRadius(70);

Add the sprite and keep in mind - now picture cannot be deleted. First it must be unloaded through the renderer: window.getRenderer()->unload(picture);. If you skip this, the image will stay in video memory.

window.add(photo);

docs.title: Final result
docs.text:
#include <Guic/Guic.hpp>

using namespace guic;

int main() {
    Window window("What's your mood?", Size(640, 480));
    window.open();

    Sprite background(Rect(0, 0, 640, 480), Color("#1b4242"));
    window.add(background);

    Image picture("kit.png");
    Sprite photo(Rect(100, 100, 140, 140), picture);
    photo.setRadius(70);
    window.add(photo);

    while (window.isOpen()) {
        window.tune();
        window.display();

        guic_delay(10);
    }

    return 0;
}
Next step – Drawing text

docs.title: Drawing text
docs.text:
To draw text, we need a font. Before the image, we create the Guic class Font, specifying the file and the size.

Font font("UbuntuMono-Bold.ttf", 16);

Fonts and text use UTF8, so, to avoid loading the whole font (which would be unreasonably expensive in RAM), we add the ready-made character sets that need to be loaded. For now, Russian and punctuation are enough

font.addPack(Font::Pack::RU);
font.addPack(Font::Pack::Sign);

Now create the text through the Guic class Text, specifying its area, the string and the font.

Text title(Rect(25, 25, 580, 40), "What kind of cat are you today?", font);

By default the font color is black. Let's take white

title.setColor(Color::White);

Add it

window.add(title);

Now let's add an answer to this question. We place the text under the picture of the cat - both on screen and in the code. The text "Need coffee and a little quiet..." will not fit in width, because the picture is much smaller. So we break the lines ourselves using \n literals

Text coffee(Rect(100, 250, 140, 60), "Need coffee\nand a little\nquiet...", font);
coffee.setColor(Color::White);
window.add(coffee);

#include <Guic/Guic.hpp>

using namespace guic;

int main() {
    Window window("What's your mood?", Size(640, 480));
    window.open();

    Sprite background(Rect(0, 0, 640, 480), Color("#1b4242"));
    window.add(background);

    Font font("UbuntuMono-Bold.ttf", 16);
    font.addPack(Font::Pack::RU);
    font.addPack(Font::Pack::Sign);

    Text title(Rect(25, 25, 580, 40), "What kind of cat are you today?", font);
    title.setColor(Color::White);
    window.add(title);

    Image picture("kit.png");
    Sprite photo(Rect(100, 100, 140, 140), picture);
    photo.setRadius(70);
    window.add(photo);

    Text coffee(Rect(100, 250, 140, 60), "Need coffee\nand a little\nquiet...", font);
    coffee.setColor(Color::White);
    window.add(coffee);

    while (window.isOpen()) {
        window.tune();
        window.display();

        guic_delay(10);
    }

    return 0;
}
Next step – Handling events

docs.title: Handling events
docs.text:
To demonstrate event handling, let's implement a like counter. We will count a click on the picture of the cat as a like. To begin with, declare the counter itself in a global variable

int likes = 0;

To handle any events, the Trigger class is used. Specify the same Rect area for the trigger as for our picture. And specify the matching rounding (make it a circle)

Trigger like(Rect(100, 100, 140, 140));
like.setRadius(70);

Now the hardest part in Guic - to set the activation condition of the trigger, you need to use a lambda function. A lambda function is a function made of three blocks:

  • Square brackets [] - used to pass external variables. We won't add anything here, but if we needed to access the trigger itself, we would write [&trigger]

  • Round brackets () - used to pass arguments. In Trigger you can either leave them empty, or add a constant pointer to an event. We add the event, because we need to catch a left mouse button press

  • Curly braces {} - the function body itself. This is where we will write the logic of the left mouse button press.

Now that we roughly understand how to use it, let's add the activation condition. * Nothing is passed in []. * In () we add a const Event* pointer to the event. * In {} we add the function body, which returns bool. Returning bool is mandatory, otherwise the code will not compile.

like.on([](const Event* event){

});

Now, when an event arrives, we need to check it, so we add our activation logic into the on function.

We are interested in the event type "mouse button click" and the specific button "left mouse button". To catch a mouse button click, we take the event type from event and compare it with the Event::EventType enumeration. To check that it is specifically the left mouse button, we take data.click.key from event.

  • *data is a variable that holds data depending on the event type. If the event type is "mouse", then event->data.key.key contains garbage. In general the order of the checks does not matter. Only reading data.text is potentially dangerous, so the event type check should be done before reading data.text.
if(event->type == Event::EventType::MouseButtonClicked && event->data.click.key == Key::LMB) {
    return true;
}

return false;
  • A MouseButtonClicked event is handled only by the element that the user originally clicked. To find such an element, the function hit(x, y) is used. For such events we can safely ignore the visible area, because a mouse click will not trigger for an element that is hidden somewhere

Hooray. We have written this monster. Its twin, bind, accepts a lambda function with no arguments or with a const Event* pointer. The version without arguments is enough here. Nothing complicated is needed, we just add one to the number of likes

like.bind([](){
    likes++;
});

Add it to the window

window.add(like);

You're a champion! Now, when the cat is clicked, the number of likes increases. This deserves a mark, and we add one more button - to reset the counter. First, the visuals:

Sprite resetShape(Rect(450, 120, 140, 50), Color("#f4e1c1"));
resetShape.setRadius(25);

Text resetCaption(Rect(480, 135, 100, 30), "Reset", font);
resetCaption.setColor(Color("#1b4242"));

And now the trigger itself. Because Guic positions itself as a convenient library, we use the ready-made onLMB() function

Trigger reset(Rect(450, 120, 140, 50));
reset.setRadius(25);
reset.onLMB([](){ likes = 0; });

An important clarification - onLMB fires on a click: the button was pressed and released over the same element - this is the standard for interfaces.

Let's display the number of likes on screen and hide the text for now. We will draw it when the first like is set.

Text total(Rect(450, 25, 280, 40), "Likes today: 0", font);
total.setColor(Color::White);
total.hide();

Add all of the above to the window

window.add(resetShape);
window.add(resetCaption);
window.add(reset);
window.add(total);

Before the loop, add a variable that will store the number of likes currently displayed. In the loop itself, after tune(), add a condition: if the number has changed, update the text and show it

int shown = 0;
while (window.isOpen()) {
    window.tune();

    if (likes != shown) {
        shown = likes;
        total.setString("Likes today: " + std::to_string(likes));
        total.show();
    }

docs.title: Structuring
docs.text:
Without structuring, a UI would be a very unusual curiosity. Fortunately, Guic provides a tool for structuring - the Container. It groups elements, passes events to them, draws them, manages their display... In short, it does everything so that you do not duplicate code for a large number of elements

Let's create this hero after adding the text about coffee:

Container container(Rect(450, 25, 280, 320));

An important clarification - the display of each element depends on its parent. When you add an element to a container, the container becomes its parent. In that case the element is clipped to its visible area, and its position is shifted relative to the parent.

Let's use this feature - remove total.hide() from the code and change the positions of the elements in Rect

Sprite resetShape(Rect(0, 95, 140, 50), Color("#f4e1c1"));
resetShape.setRadius(25);

Text resetCaption(Rect(30, 110, 100, 30), "Reset", font);
resetCaption.setColor(Color("#1b4242"));

Trigger reset(Rect(0, 95, 140, 50));
reset.setRadius(25);
reset.onLMB([](){ likes = 0; });

Text total(Rect(0, 0, 280, 40), "Likes today: 0", font);
total.setColor(Color::White);

Now we change the logic of showing the counter. From now on, both the button and the number of likes will be displayed only if the user has clicked the cat. Add all the elements to the container, hide the container, and add the container itself to the window:

container.add(resetShape);
container.add(resetCaption);
container.add(reset);
container.add(total);
container.hide();

window.add(container);

And instead of the function that showed the counter, we will now show the container

container.show();
